rationale: A wins because it found the sharpest business story and framed it for the right desk: "The poster child of online-only retail now runs more than 300 stores" is an actual thesis a retail reporter can test. B has good bones, but "Warby Parker says store shoppers spend more than online buyers. It will not say how much." mistakes an unquantified company claim for a data angle; that is not a scoop, it is homework. A also had the discipline to refuse that same weak standalone data play.
gaps_in_A: "Warby Parker was the canonical example of that thesis" leans on outside reputation, not the supplied update. Probably true, but still needs sourcing before it goes into a pitch.
"pharmacy chains' fight to reinvent the front of store" is an outside trend peg the update did not supply. Use it only if you can prove it with current reporting.
"the death of a retail thesis" is a little too neat. One Warby expansion is strong evidence against online-only purity; it does not bury an entire thesis by itself.
gaps_in_B: "Warby Parker says store shoppers spend more than online buyers. It will not say how much." is not a standalone data angle without the number. It is a proof request pretending to be a story.

"Direct-to-consumer brands are all going physical, and Warby Parker proves it" gets refused as a duplicate, but that throws away the strongest contrarian retail lens. It is not the same protagonist as the spend metric.
"puts pressure on whoever currently sells eyewear in pharmacies and on incumbent optical chains" invents competitive impact the update does not prove.
"The category question stays open for as long as the rollout is under way" stretches the why-now. The announcement is fresh; the rollout itself is not a blank check for urgency.
